images.title: Make the divisor whole
images.purpose: Show that multiplying the dividend and the divisor by the same 10 or 100 turns a decimal divisor into a counting number without changing the quotient.
images.composition: Two short rows stacked in the centre, each a pair of divisions joined by an arrow, with white space between the rows.
exact_structure: Row 1 left: 4.68 ÷ 1.3; a teal #0072B2 arrow to the right labelled × 10 both; row 1 right: 46.8 ÷ 13 = 3.6.
Row 2 left: 4.68 ÷ 0.13; an amber #E69F00 arrow to the right labelled × 100 both; row 2 right: 468 ÷ 13 = 36.
In both rows the divisor 13 on the right is circled in reddish purple #CC79A7.
The two answers 3.6 and 36 are in green #009E73.
rejection: a multiplier other than × 10 in row 1 or × 100 in row 2
only the divisor changed and the dividend left as 4.68 on the right side
images.takeaway: Multiply both numbers by the same 10 or 100 until the divisor is a counting number, then divide.
images.description: Two rows: 4.68 ÷ 1.3 becomes 46.8 ÷ 13 = 3.6 after multiplying both by 10, and 4.68 ÷ 0.13 becomes 468 ÷ 13 = 36 after multiplying both by 100.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on making the divisor a counting number.
images.teaching_notes: Ask students why the dividend must change too, and compare the two answers.

image_decisions.why: The two side by side rewrites show the rule at a glance.
